lesson.title: Pattern Recognition: Spotting Repetition Before You Automate It
lesson.summary: Teaches how to notice repeated structure and similarity within a problem, and how recognizing a pattern leads directly to writing a loop instead of repetitive code.
lesson.body:
Pattern recognition, in computer science, means noticing similarities: between the current problem and one you have solved before, or between different parts of the same problem. It matters because computers are extremely good at doing the exact same thing over and over, and a programmer's job is often to spot when a task is "the same step, repeated" so that repetition can be automated rather than typed out by hand. Humans are naturally decent at this kind of noticing in everyday life, recognizing a familiar melody after just a few notes or a familiar face across a crowded room, and computational thinking asks you to apply that same instinct deliberately to code.

Imagine printing a small multiplication table for the numbers 1 through 4. A programmer without pattern recognition might start typing individual print statements: print(1*1), print(1*2), and so on, quickly producing sixteen nearly identical lines. Someone applying pattern recognition instead notices that every entry follows the exact same rule: the value in row r and column c is always r times c. Once that pattern is named, it can be captured with a loop instead of copied by hand:

for row in range(1, 5):
    for col in range(1, 5):
        print(row * col, end=" ")
    print()

Tracing the outer loop, row takes the values 1, 2, 3, and 4 in turn. For each row, the inner loop runs col through 1, 2, 3, and 4, printing row * col each time with a space instead of a newline. When row is 3, the inner loop prints 3, 6, 9, 12. After the inner loop finishes, the plain print() call adds a newline so the next row starts fresh. The result is a 4 by 4 grid of products, produced by two lines of looping logic instead of sixteen separate print statements, purely because the repeated pattern, row times col, was recognized and generalized.

Pattern recognition connects closely to both decomposition and algorithms. After decomposition breaks a problem into pieces, pattern recognition often reveals that several of those pieces are actually the same underlying task performed on different data, which is exactly what justifies writing a loop, or a reusable function, instead of duplicated code. It also connects backward to earlier work: the linear search algorithm from an earlier section is itself a recognized pattern, "check one item, then move to the next," reused any time you need to scan through a collection.

Beyond code, pattern recognition is a habit worth building deliberately. When you approach a new problem, ask whether it resembles something you have already solved, even partially. A problem asking you to find the smallest value in a list is nearly identical in structure to the "find the largest value" example from the introduction to computer science, except for a single flipped comparison. Recognizing that similarity means you do not have to design a solution from scratch, you can adapt one you already trust. Over time, this is how experienced programmers build up a mental library of recognizable shapes, scanning a list, comparing pairs, accumulating a running total, so that a new problem rarely feels completely unfamiliar.
